The interpretation, supported by matched comparisons

Under our tested conditions, scores were mostly unchanged by name, location, and university variations, but some resumes showed sensitivity to these attributes. Qualification differences were substantially larger on average.

How we isolate an attribute: compare each variant with its designated reference resume, holding the job, qualification profile, and other identity fields fixed. Match run 1 with run 1, run 2 with run 2, and run 3 with run 3. For a resume’s average score, average all three runs on each side first, then subtract.

1. “Mostly unchanged”: around 90% of matched run scores were identical

These percentages compare individual runs with the same seed. They describe this dataset; repeated comparisons share resumes and references and are not independent applicants.

2. “Some sensitivity”: small average differences can hide larger cases

Here each comparison uses a resume variant’s three-run average minus its reference’s three-run average. “Average size” uses absolute differences, so increases and decreases cannot cancel each other out.

The 8 name and 1 university interview changes are individual same-seed comparisons crossing the fixed 70-point cutoff; they are not counts of unique applicants. One university version is excluded from this matched analysis because one of its runs had an invalid category score. Its raw response remains in the full results below.

3. “Qualifications mattered more on average”: a much larger designed gap

25.36 points

Average higher-minus-lower qualification difference across 200 matched version pairs. Higher scored more in 199 pairs, and one tied.

These pairs hold the tested attribute and profile fixed. One pair uses two valid runs on one side. This is a designed qualification contrast, not a name or location test.

0.65–0.84 points

Average absolute change in three-run mean scores when varying a name, location, or university against the reference, with qualifications fixed.

The comparisons answer different questions. Their descriptive magnitudes support “larger on average,” not a universal ranking of real-world influences.

What we can—and cannot—conclude: this is descriptive evidence of mostly unchanged scores with occasional attribute sensitivity. No significance test or equivalence test has been performed. The results do not prove no effect, establish systematic favoritism toward a demographic group, or generalize beyond this model, prompts, and selected variants. Names are socially associated signals, not verified identities. Locations are the selected Massachusetts variants, not a national or international sample. Score sensitivity also needs to be interpreted against the observed variation across repeated runs.

How interview decisions are calculated

Score ≥ 70 → yes. Score < 70 → no. The page shows only this calculated decision. It does not change the model’s saved score or justification.

Use the original numerical scores to analyze sensitivity to names, locations, and universities. Calculated interview decisions show whether score differences cross the fixed cutoff. The range-invalid score remains flagged for review. Original model answers remain in the saved research data.

Higher qualification   Lower qualification. Data-analysis higher averages use 149 responses; every other group uses 150.

Administration needs careful interpretation. Using the 70-point rule, 123 of 150 lower-qualification administration evaluations receive an interview decision of yes. Those profiles may still fit entry-level administrative work. That finding alone does not establish an error or justify changing the threshold afterward.
